units.title: Scientific Learning
topics: Scientific study and the scientific method
Variables in scientific research: independent, dependent and controlled variables
Fundamental and derived units and their analysis
Unit-wise analysis of equations and scientific investigation
summary: Science is the organised study of nature through observation and experiment; technology applies scientific knowledge to solve problems.
The scientific method: problem → observation → hypothesis → experiment → data analysis → conclusion → report.
In an experiment there is one independent variable, a dependent variable that we measure, and controlled variables kept constant; a control group is used for comparison.
Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated readings. Taking the mean of several readings reduces random error.
SI base units: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), kelvin (K), ampere (A), candela (cd), mole (mol). Going to a smaller unit, multiply; to a bigger unit, divide.
Least count of a vernier = 1 MSD − 1 VSD (usually 0.01 cm); of a screw gauge = pitch / number of circular divisions (usually 0.01 mm).
Density = mass / volume; km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18.
A project follows these steps: topic, plan, data collection, analysis, conclusion, report. A report has an introduction, methods, analysis, conclusion and references.

units.title: Classification of Living Beings
topics: Five-kingdom classification and taxonomic hierarchy
Kingdom Plantae: Algae, Bryophyta and Tracheophyta (Pteridophyta, Gymnosperms and Angiosperms)
Kingdom Animalia: eight invertebrate phyla and Phylum Chordata (five classes of Vertebrata)
Relationship between classification and evolution

sections.title: Characteristics of Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia

summary: Taxonomy is the identification, naming and classification of organisms. Linnaeus is the father of taxonomy; Whittaker proposed five kingdoms in 1969.
The hierarchy is Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species; the species is the basic unit.
Binomial nomenclature: two Latin names, genus (capital) then species (small letter), in italics or underlined.
Monera: prokaryotic, unicellular (bacteria, cyanobacteria); binary fission.
Protista: unicellular eukaryotes (Amoeba, Paramecium, Euglena).
Fungi: chitin cell wall, hyphae, saprophytic or parasitic, spores (yeast, mushroom).
Plantae: multicellular, cellulose wall, photosynthesis; algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms, angiosperms.
Animalia: multicellular, heterotrophic, no cell wall; invertebrate phyla and five classes of vertebrates (fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals).

units.title: Honey Bee
topics: Types of honey bees, castes and external structure
Life cycle (egg, larva, pupa, adult), nuptial flight and parthenogenesis (2n=32, n=16)
Colony organisation, age-wise division of labour of worker bees and bee dances
Apiculture (bee keeping), honey, royal jelly, beeswax and pollination
summary: Honey bees belong to genus Apis, class Insecta, order Hymenoptera. Wild species: A. dorsata, A. laboriosa, A. florea; domesticated: A. cerana, A. mellifera.
The colony has three castes: one queen (fertile female), thousands of workers (sterile females) and drones (males).
Life cycle: egg → larva → pupa → adult (complete metamorphosis). Egg-to-adult time: queen 16 days, worker 21 days, drone 24 days.
Fertilised eggs give queens and workers (diet decides which); unfertilised eggs give drones (parthenogenesis).
Division of labour among workers by age: cleaner, nurse, house bee (comb builder), guard, forager. Bees communicate by round and waggle dances.
The comb is made of hexagonal wax cells; the brood is at the centre, pollen around it and honey above.
Bee-keeping tools: movable-frame hive, queen excluder, smoker, veil, hive tool, honey extractor.
Products: honey, beeswax, royal jelly, propolis, pollen and bee venom. Bees also pollinate crops.

units.title: Heredity
topics: Mendel's experiments and laws of inheritance
Cell division (mitosis and meiosis), chromosomes, DNA, RNA and genes
Sex determination in humans
Genetic disorders and genetic technology (selective breeding, AI, IVF and DNA testing)

sections.title: Cell division (mitosis and meiosis), chromosomes, DNA, RNA and genes

summary: Heredity is the passing of characters from parents to offspring through genes. Mendel, the father of genetics, worked with pea plants and discovered the laws of inheritance.
Monohybrid cross Tt × Tt gives phenotypic ratio 3 : 1 and genotypic ratio 1 : 2 : 1; a test cross with the recessive parent shows whether a dominant plant is pure.
Dihybrid cross RrYy × RrYy gives 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
Laws: dominance, segregation (purity of gametes), independent assortment.
Cell → nucleus → chromosome → DNA → gene. Humans have 46 chromosomes (22 pairs autosomes + XX or XY). DNA is a double helix with A–T and C–G pairing.
Sex is decided by the father's sperm: X-sperm gives a girl, Y-sperm gives a boy; chance 50 : 50.
Sex-linked recessive disorders (colour blindness, haemophilia) are commoner in males.
Chromosomal disorders: Down's (47, trisomy 21), Turner's (XO, 45), Klinefelter's (XXY, 47). Genetic counselling helps prevention.

units.title: Physiological Structure and Life Process
topics: Human blood: composition, blood cells and functions
Structure and working of the human heart
Blood vessels and double circulation
Blood groups, blood pressure, heart attack and angiography
Diabetes (hyperglycemia) and uric acid (gout)

sections.title: Human blood: composition, blood cells and functions
Structure and working of the human heart
Blood groups, blood pressure, heart attack and angiography

summary: Human blood (5–5.5 L, pH 7.4): Plasma (55%) + Blood cells (45%): RBCs / Erythrocytes (4.5–5.5 million/mm^3, biconcave, non-nucleated, haemoglobin carries O2, lifespan 120 days, deficiency causes anaemia); WBCs / Leucocytes (4,000–11,000/mm^3, nucleated, fight germs, uncontrolled excess causes leukaemia, deficiency causes leukopenia); Plat

Human heart: Protected by double-layered pericardium with pericardial fluid. Four chambers: Right Auricle, Right Ventricle (deoxygenated blood) and Left Auricle, Left Ventricle (oxygenated blood; thickest wall to pump blood to the whole body). Four valves: tricuspid, bicuspid (mitral), pulmonary semilunar and aortic semilunar.

Blood vessels: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure (thick elastic wall, narrow lumen, no valves; exception: pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood). Veins carry blood towards the heart under low pressure (thin wall, wide lumen, have valves; exception: pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood). Capillaries are o
Double circulation: Pulmonary (RV → Pulmonary artery → Lungs → Pulmonary veins → LA) and Systemic (LV → Aorta → Body → Vena cava → RA).
Blood pressure: Normal adult value 120/80 mm Hg (systolic/diastolic), measured by a sphygmomanometer.

Heart attack: Blockage of coronary arteries by cholesterol plaque/clot. Angiogram (coronary angiography) locates the blockage using contrast dye and X-rays; treated by angioplasty/stent or open-heart bypass surgery (CABG).

Diabetes (hyperglycemia): Excess blood glucose due to insulin deficiency; causes frequent urination, thirst, hunger and slow wound healing. Uric acid (gout): Excess purine breakdown product forms urate crystals in joints (big toe), controlled by drinking plenty of water and avoiding red meat and alcohol.

units.title: Nature and Environment
topics: Ecosystem and natural balance
Environmental pollution and acid rain
Greenhouse effect and climate change
Waste management
Conservation, endangered species and medicinal plants of Nepal
summary: An ecosystem is the living (producers, consumers, decomposers) and non-living parts of a place interacting. Energy flows in one direction (10% passes to the next level); matter is recycled in carbon, nitrogen and water cycles.
Food chains join to form a food web: producer → herbivore → carnivore → top carnivore.

Air pollutants: CO, CO₂, SO₂, NOₓ, particles, CFCs; water pollution from sewage, chemicals and fertilisers (eutrophication); soil pollution from plastic and agrochemicals; noise above 85 dB harms hearing.

Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, CFCs) trap heat. Global warming melts glaciers, raises sea level and changes rainfall. CFCs thin the ozone layer, allowing more UV rays; the Montreal Protocol controls them.
Waste is biodegradable or non-biodegradable. Follow the 3 Rs (reduce, reuse, recycle) and segregate at source; compost, biogas and sanitary landfill are the main treatments.
Conservation is wise use of resources: in-situ (parks, reserves, community forests) and ex-situ (zoos, gene banks). Nepal protects about 23% of its land; Chitwan was the first national park (1973).

units.title: Motion and Force
topics: Force, inertia, Newton's laws of motion and momentum
Universal law of gravitation and properties/effects of gravitation
Gravity, acceleration due to gravity (g), feather-coin experiment and variation of g
Mass, weight and weightlessness
Free fall, equations of motion under gravity and parachute motion
summary: Force is a push or a pull; unit newton. Net force zero means the forces are balanced.
Newton's first law: a body keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless an unbalanced force acts. Inertia depends on mass.
Newton's second law: F = ma; also F = dfracΔ pt. 1 N gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻².
Newton's third law: action and reaction are equal and opposite and act on different bodies.
Momentum p = mv (kg m s⁻¹); impulse Ft = mv - mu. Without external force, m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2.
Gravitation: F = Gdfracm1 m2d^2 with G = 6.67×10^-11 N m² kg⁻²; g = dfracGMR^2 = 9.8 m s⁻²; g is greatest at the poles and zero at the Earth's centre.
Weight W = mg (newton) changes from place to place; mass (kg) does not.
Free fall: v = gt, h = tfrac12 gt^2, v^2 = 2gh; for upward throw H = dfracu^22g, time of flight dfrac2ug.

units.title: Pressure
topics: Thrust and pressure in solids, liquids and gases
Pascal's law and hydraulic machines (hydraulic lift, brake and excavator)
Atmospheric pressure, syringe, air pump and water hand pump
Upthrust, Archimedes' principle and the law of floatation

sections.title: Pressure in solids, liquids and gases
Atmospheric pressure, syringe, air pump and water hand pump

summary: Pressure = thrust ÷ area: P = F/A; unit pascal (1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²). Small area gives high pressure.
Liquid pressure: P = hρ g; it increases with depth and acts equally in all directions at a point.
Pascal's law: pressure on an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions. Hydraulic machine: F = f (A/a).
Atmospheric pressure at sea level = 76 cm Hg = 1.013×10^5 Pa; it decreases with altitude. A barometer measures it.
Archimedes' principle: upthrust = weight of fluid displaced = Vρ g; apparent weight = weight − upthrust.
A body sinks if ρb > ρl, floats if ρb < ρl; for a floating body, upthrust = weight.
Ships float because their average density is less than water's; submarines, hydrometers and balloons use the same law.

units.title: Heat
topics: Heat energy, temperature, anomalous expansion of water and Hope's apparatus
Specific heat capacity, Q = mcΔ T, calorimetry and metal-balls wax experiment
Change of state, latent heat and calibration of a thermometer
Modes of heat transfer and the thermos flask
summary: Heat is energy (joule); temperature tells hotness. Heat flows from higher to lower temperature. T(K) = t(°C) + 273.
Linear expansion: Δ L = α L0 Δ T. Bimetallic strips, rail gaps and tyre-fitting use expansion.
Water contracts from 0 °C to 4 °C and has maximum density at 4 °C; this saves aquatic life in frozen lakes.
Specific heat capacity c: heat to raise 1 kg by 1 °C; Q = mcΔ T (water c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹). Heat lost = heat gained in mixing.
Latent heat: Q = mL with no change in temperature. Lf(ice) = 3.36×10^5 J kg⁻¹, Lv(water) = 2.26×10^6 J kg⁻¹.
Conduction (solids, particles vibrate), convection (fluids, particles move), radiation (waves, no medium needed).
Dull black surfaces absorb and emit heat well; shiny surfaces reflect heat. A thermos flask reduces all three modes.

units.title: Wave
topics: Wave motion and electromagnetic waves
Sound waves and their characteristics
Refraction of light, total internal reflection, critical angle, optical fibre and dispersion
Convex and concave lenses, ray diagrams, lens formula, magnification and power
Human eye, defects of vision (myopia and hypermetropia), cataract and corneal transplantation
summary: A wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Transverse: vibration ⟂ wave direction; longitudinal: vibration ∥ wave direction. v = fλ, T = 1/f.
Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave; cannot travel in a vacuum; fastest in solids. Audible range 20 Hz–20 kHz. Echo needs at least 17 m: d = vt/2.
Loudness depends on amplitude, pitch on frequency, quality on waveform.
Reflection: ∠ i = ∠ r. Mirror formula dfrac1f = dfrac1u + dfrac1v, f = R/2, m = v/u.
Refraction: dfracsin isin r = n = dfraccv; total internal reflection when light goes dense → rare with i > C, where sin C = 1/n.
Lens formula dfrac1f = dfrac1u + dfrac1v; power P = 1/f (m) in dioptre; convex is positive, concave is negative.
Myopia is corrected by a concave lens, hypermetropia by a convex lens. Compound microscope and telescope use two convex lenses.

units.title: Electricity and Magnetism
topics: Electric current, potential difference and Ohm's law
Resistance and combination of resistors
Electrical power, energy consumption and household wiring safety
Direct current (DC), alternating current (AC, 50 Hz), magnetic effect of current and motor effect
Magnetic flux and Faraday's laws of electromagnetic induction
AC generator (dynamo), bicycle dynamo and step-up/step-down transformers

sections.title: Direct Current (DC), Alternating Current (AC) and Magnetic Effect of Current

summary: I = Q/t (A); V = work per unit charge (V). Ohm's law: V = IR at constant temperature.
R = ρ l/A. Series: Rs = R1 + R2 + cdots; parallel: dfrac1Rp = dfrac1R1 + dfrac1R2 + cdots.
Power P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R; energy W = Pt; 1 kWh = 3.6×10⁶ J. Heat H = I^2Rt. A fuse breaks an overloaded circuit.
A current produces a magnetic field (Oersted). Right-hand grip rule gives its direction; a solenoid with an iron core is an electromagnet.
A conductor carrying current in a magnetic field feels a force (Fleming's left-hand rule). The DC motor uses it and a split-ring commutator.
Electromagnetic induction: changing flux induces an emf (Faraday); its direction opposes the change (Lenz). Fleming's right-hand rule gives the direction.
AC generator: mechanical → electrical energy, slip rings, output AC (50 Hz in Nepal).
Transformer (AC only): dfracVsVp = dfracNsNp and VpIp = VsIs for an ideal one; high-voltage transmission reduces I^2R loss.

units.title: Universe
topics: Universe and the importance of gravitational force
Big Bang theory and Hubble's study
Future of the universe: open, flat and closed universe and Big Crunch

sections.title: Universe and the importance of gravitational force
Big Bang theory and Hubble's study
Future of the universe: open, flat and closed universe and Big Crunch

summary: Gravitational force forms stars from nebulae, binds stars into galaxies and galaxy clusters, keeps planets and satellites in orbit, retains Earth's atmosphere/hydrosphere, and governs the future fate of the universe.
The universe is everything that exists. 1 light year = 9.46×10^12 km (distance); 1 AU = 1.5×10^8 km.
Big Bang theory: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense singularity and has been expanding and cooling ever since.

Hubble's law: The recession velocity (v) of a distant galaxy is directly proportional to its distance (d): v = Hd, where H ≈ 70–73.8 km s^-1Mpc^-1 is the Hubble constant. Spectral redshift proves galaxies are moving apart.
Critical density (ρc ≈ (1–3)× 10^-26 kg m^-3): The boundary density at which gravity just balances expansion.

Future of the universe: Open universe (ρ < ρc) expands forever; Flat universe (ρ = ρc) expands at a decreasing rate approaching zero at infinity; Closed universe (ρ > ρc) stops expanding and contracts back into a singularity (Big Crunch).
Satellites stay in orbit because gravity supplies the centripetal force. Geostationary satellites orbit at 36,000 km with a 24 h period; NepaliSat-1 (2019) was Nepal's first satellite.

units.title: Information and Communication Technology
topics: Signals, analog-to-digital conversion and memory units
Signal transmission and digital communication system
Impact of digital technology in daily life
Digital citizenship, online reputation and digital wellbeing
Creating and editing audio and audio-visual materials

sections.title: Signals, analog-to-digital conversion and memory units
Signal transmission and digital communication system
Impact of digital technology in daily life
Digital citizenship, online reputation and digital wellbeing
Creating and editing audio and audio-visual materials

summary: A signal is a time-varying physical quantity that carries information. Analog signals are continuous sine waves; digital signals are discrete binary pulses (0 = LOW / switch OFF, 1 = HIGH / switch ON).
An ADC converts analog signals into digital binary code; a DAC converts digital binary data back into analog signals for human perception.

Computer memory units: 1 bit = 0 or 1 (smallest unit); 1 nibble = 4 bits; 1 Byte (B) = 8 bits = 2 nibbles (e.g. 00000000); 1 KB = 1024 B; 1 MB = 1024 KB; 1 GB = 1024 MB; 1 TB = 1024 GB. With n bits, 2^n binary combinations are possible.
Stages of digital signal transmission (in order): Source → Input Transducer → Encoder → Modulator → Channel → Demodulator → Decoder → Output Transducer → Output Signal.

Baseband transmission sends digital signals directly without modulation over a single short-distance channel (Ethernet LAN). Broadband transmission modulates signals onto multiple carrier frequencies (FDM) to send many signals simultaneously over long distances (cable TV, high-speed internet).

Netizen = an active user ("citizen") of the internet. Digital citizenship = responsible, ethical and safe participation online. Online reputation management builds and protects a person's or organisation's public image online.
Digital wellbeing is maintaining physical, mental, social and emotional health by balancing online screen time with offline life.
Audio formats: .mp3, .wav, .wma, .aac (edited in Audacity). Video formats: .mp4, .3gp, .avi, .svi, .mov (trimmed and joined in Windows Video Editor, Filmora or Premiere Pro).
terms: Online Reputation and Digital Reputation Management

units.title: Classification of Elements
topics: Mendeleev's and Modern Periodic Table (blocks s, p, d, f; lanthanides and actinides)
Electronic configuration and periodic trends (atomic size, valency, electronegativity and reactivity)
Groups, periods and position of metals, non-metals and metalloids
summary: Dobereiner (triads), Newlands (octaves) and Mendeleev (periodic law by atomic mass) were early attempts; Moseley's modern periodic law uses atomic number.
The modern table has 18 groups and 7 periods; blocks are s, p, d and f.
Period number = number of shells; group number (1, 2) = valence electrons; groups 13 to 18: valence electrons + 10.
Valency = valence electrons (1 to 3) or 8 − valence electrons (4 to 7); noble gases are 0.
Down a group: atomic size increases; ionisation energy and electronegativity decrease; metallic character increases.
Across a period: atomic size decreases; ionisation energy and electronegativity increase; non-metallic character increases.
Group 1 = alkali metals, group 2 = alkaline earth metals, group 17 = halogens, group 18 = noble gases.

units.title: Chemical Reaction
topics: Types of chemical reactions (combination, decomposition, displacement, acid-base and exothermic/endothermic)
Word equations, formula equations and balancing chemical equations
Rate of chemical reaction and factors affecting reaction rate (temperature, pressure, surface area, light and catalysts)
Neutralisation reactions and everyday applications of acids, bases and salts
summary: A chemical reaction forms new substances; it is shown by a balanced equation (reactants → products).
Types: combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement, exothermic/endothermic and redox.
Mass is conserved: balance equations by writing coefficients, never by changing subscripts.
Rate of reaction increases with concentration, surface area, temperature and a catalyst.
Acids give H⁺, bases (alkalis) give OH⁻; pH below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is basic.
Acid + base → salt + water is neutralisation; Acid + metal → salt + H₂; Acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO₂.
Important salts: NaCl, NaHCO₃, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, plaster of Paris, bleaching powder.
terms: Catalyst: Positive Catalyst and Negative Catalyst

topics: Carbon dioxide gas: laboratory preparation, properties and uses
Ammonia gas: laboratory preparation, Haber's process, properties and uses
Greenhouse effect and acid rain

sections.title: Carbon dioxide gas: laboratory preparation, properties and uses
Ammonia gas: laboratory preparation, Haber's process, properties and uses

summary: Carbon dioxide (CO2, mol. mass 44): Prepared in the lab at room temperature from marble chips and dilute HCl: CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2 uparrow. Collected in an upright jar by upward displacement of air (1.5× heavier than air, soluble in water).

Key reactions of CO2: Dissolves in water to form H2CO3; turns lime water milky (CaCO3 downarrow) on short passing and colourless (Ca(HCO3)2) in excess; burning Mg continues to burn in CO2 (2Mg + CO2 → 2MgO + C); reacts with NH3 under heat and pressure to form urea (NH2CONH2).

Ammonia (NH3, mol. mass 17): Prepared in the lab by heating NH4Cl and Ca(OH)2 (2:1): 2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 xrightarrowΔ CaCl2 + 2H2O + 2NH3 uparrow. Dried through a quicklime (CaO) tower and collected in an inverted jar by downward displacement of air (lighter than air and extremely soluble in water).
Haber's process: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 + Heat at 450–500 ^circC, 200–900 atm, with Fe catalyst and Mo promoter.

Tests for NH3: Turns moist red litmus blue; forms dense white fumes of NH4Cl with conc. HCl; turns Nessler's reagent brown. The fountain experiment demonstrates its extreme solubility in water and alkaline nature.
Greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, N2O, CFCs, H2O) trap infrared heat; excess emissions cause global warming. Acid rain (H2SO4, H2SO3, HNO3 from SO2 and NOx) corrodes monuments and acidifies soil and water.

units.title: Metal and Non-metals
topics: Physical and chemical properties of metals and non-metals
Reactivity series and displacement reactions
Minerals, ores of Fe, Al, Cu, Ag and Au, and the five steps of metallurgy
Corrosion and rusting of iron
summary: Metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile and conduct heat and electricity; non-metals are dull, brittle and poor conductors (graphite and diamond are exceptions).
Metal oxides are basic; non-metal oxides are acidic; Al₂O₃ and ZnO are amphoteric.
Reactivity series: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Hg, Ag, Au. A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one; only metals above H liberate H₂ from dilute acids.
Ores of Fe: haematite and magnetite; Al: bauxite; Cu: copper pyrite.
Steps: crushing, concentration, calcination/roasting, reduction, refining. Reactive metals are extracted by electrolysis; middle metals by carbon reduction.
Iron is made in a blast furnace from haematite, coke and limestone; Al is extracted by electrolysis of alumina in cryolite.
Rusting needs oxygen and water; prevent it by painting, galvanising, plating and alloying.

units.title: Hydrocarbon and its Compounds
topics: Saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons (alkanes, alkenes, alkynes) and methane, ethane, propane and butane
Homologous series, alkyl radicals and functional groups
Monohydric, dihydric and trihydric alcohols: methanol, ethanol and glycerol
Organic acids and everyday organic compounds

sections.title: Alcohols: monohydric, dihydric and trihydric alcohols (methanol, ethanol and glycerol)

summary: Carbon is tetravalent and shows catenation; hydrocarbons contain only C and H.
Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (single bonds, substitution); alkenes CₙH₂ₙ (C=C, addition and polymerisation); alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (C≡C, addition).
Unsaturated hydrocarbons decolourise bromine water and Baeyer's reagent; alkanes do not.
A homologous series has the same functional group and general formula, and members differ by –CH₂– (14 u).
Alcohols CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH (–OH): ethanol is made by fermentation of sugar; it reacts with Na to give H₂; oxidises to ethanoic acid; methanol is poisonous.
Carboxylic acids CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH (–COOH): ethanoic acid (vinegar) is a weak acid, gives CO₂ with NaHCO₃, and forms esters with alcohols.

units.title: Chemicals used in Daily Life
topics: Food preservatives and artificial fruit ripening agents
Cleaning chemicals: soap, detergent and natural cleansers
Pesticides: chemical and biological pesticides and safety precautions
Chemical pollution and its management

sections.title: Food preservatives and artificial fruit ripening agents
Cleaning chemicals: soap, detergent and natural cleansers
Pesticides: chemical and biological pesticides and safety precautions

summary: Food preservatives prevent microbial spoilage of food. Natural preservatives (salt, sugar, mustard oil, vinegar, lemon juice, spices, sun-drying, freezing) are safe and eco-friendly; chemical preservatives (sodium benzoate, SO2, potassium metabisulphite, sorbates, calcium propionate, BHA, BHT) must be used only within safe limits.

Artificial fruit ripening: Calcium carbide (CaC2) releases acetylene gas and contains toxic arsenic/phosphorus impurities (banned/harmful); ethylene gas (C2H4) and regulated ethephon are safer alternatives.

Soap is the sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain fatty acid (e.g. sodium stearate, C17H35COONa), prepared by saponification (heating vegetable oil or animal fat with NaOH/KOH and adding NaCl to precipitate solid soap, leaving glycerol as by-product).

Detergent ("soapless soap") is a synthetic petrochemical salt of alkyl benzene sulphonic acid or alkyl sulphate (e.g. sodium lauryl sulphate). It works in both hard and soft water without forming scum, but non-biodegradable detergents cause water pollution and eutrophication.

Pesticides: Insecticides (DDT, BHC, Malathion, Aldrin, Dieldrin), Fungicides (Bordeaux mixture, Mancozeb), Herbicides (2,4-D, Glyphosate), Rodenticides (Zinc phosphide), Miticides (Dicofol). Biological pesticides (Neem, Titepati, Bt) are target-specific and biodegradable.

Store and use pesticides strictly under the Pesticides Management Act 2076 with PPE, proper labelling and waiting periods. Manage non-biodegradable pollutants (plastics, glass, ceramics, synthetic fibres) through the 3R principle and proper waste segregation.
